[system]: New matter – Orion Components LLC v. Delta Industrial Supply Co. (State trial court).

Client summary (prepared by intake paralegal based on client call): Orion manufactures custom control panels. The contract price and delivery schedule were specified, and there is a clause stating: "In no event shall either party be liable for any consequential, incidental, or special damages, including lost profits, arising out of or related to this Agreement." Orion says Delta repeatedly delivered shipments 3–6 weeks late over a six-month period, despite Orion’s complaints. Orion claims it lost several major sales because it could not complete control panels on time and is seeking substantial lost-profit damages. Delta admits some delays but says they were due to supply-chain disruptions and argues that the limitation-of-liability clause bars Orion’s claim for lost profits. There is no allegation of personal injury or property damage.

No copy of the actual contract or prior correspondence is available yet; we only have this summary.

Please act as a junior lawyer assisting the team by focusing only on the following issue: Based on mainstream principles in a typical U.S. state contract law jurisdiction, and given only the facts above, how likely is a court to enforce the quoted limitation-of-liability clause to preclude Orion from recovering lost-profit damages, assuming the clause is clearly worded and was part of a negotiated commercial agreement between sophisticated parties? rounds.response: Short answer: a court in a typical U.S. commercial-law jurisdiction is more likely than not to enforce the clear, mutual, negotiated exclusion of "consequential... including lost profits" and bar Orion’s lost‑profit recovery, subject to several important caveats. Governing tests the court will apply include (1) the UCC standard for contractual limits on remedies (parties may validly limit consequential damages unless the clause is unconscionable or the limited remedy fails of its essential purpose), (2) common‑law doctrines of unconscionability, ambiguity, or public‑policy invalidation, and (3) recognized exceptions where a party’s intentional, fraudulent, or willful misconduct (or a complete failure of the contract’s essential remedy) makes enforcement unjust. Applying those tests to the facts given, enforcement looks likely because the clause is clear, bilateral, and negotiated between sophisticated commercial parties and there is no allegation of personal injury or special statutory protection; unconscionability is unlikely on the face of these facts. Major uncertainties that should be investigated before a firm position: the actual contract language (any carve‑outs for fraud/willful misconduct, notice/limitation formalities, force‑majeure and excuse provisions, integration language), precise facts about Delta’s conduct (was the breach willful, fraudulent, or did remedies effectively fail?), whether the lost profits arguably constitute direct rather than consequential damages under the contract, and any applicable state UCC/case law nuances. Recommendation: obtain the full contract and documentary evidence of the negotiations and the nature of Delta’s delays to evaluate the narrow factual triggers that can defeat an otherwise enforceable limitation clause.

rounds.response: Below is an ordered outline of the key factual and contractual issues to obtain and review first, with a one‑line note on how each could strengthen or weaken enforcement of the quoted exclusion of lost profits. 1) Exact clause text and placement (including any carve‑outs for fraud/willful misconduct or express savings language): a clear, unambiguous exclusion that expressly covers “lost profits” and is in the integrated agreement strengthens enforcement; ambiguous wording or an explicit carve‑out weakens it. 2) Integration/entire‑agreement and signature blocks plus any contemporaneous purchase orders or amendments: an integration clause/evidence of mutual signatures and lack of conflicting documents strengthens enforcement; prior written terms or subsequent confirmations that promise different remedies weaken it. 3) Other remedial provisions (exclusive remedies, liquidated damages, cure/notice requirements) and any procedural prerequisites: a mutually exclusive remedies clause or explicit cure/notice mechanics that Orion failed to follow may bolster enforcement; contrasting remedies or an inadequate/failed contractual remedy may undermine it. 4) Applicable law/UCC treatment (if sale of goods), force‑majeure or excuse clauses, and evidence about negotiation/sophistication: under UCC 2‑719 parties can limit consequential damages—fact of negotiation and sophistication supports enforcement, whereas a showing the limited remedy “failed of its essential purpose,” or that Delta engaged in grossly negligent, fraudulent, or willful conduct would tend to prevent enforcement. 5) Factual matrix around the delays (frequency, length, reasons, contemporaneous complaints and Delta’s responses) and the character of Orion’s lost profits (foreseeable/direct vs. consequential under Hadley principles): short, inadvertent delays attributed to supply‑chain problems with prompt cure efforts support enforcement; a sustained pattern of deliberate breaches, concealment, or objective evidence that the contract allocated direct lost‑profit risk to Delta (or that the contract’s remedy was practically worthless) weakens it—obtain the contract, POs, and correspondence immediately to test these points.
